name: metapool
workload: Construction and reserve() of mtp::vault (pool-backed dynamic array) vs std::vector (std::allocator/ptmalloc) and std::pmr::vector (pmr pool + monotonic_buffer_resource), across element counts.
claimed_speedup: README headline: up to 1300x faster construction and reserve() than std::vector and up to 3.5x faster than std::pmr::vector. Results image: reserve microbenchmark 939.81x-1380.19x faster than std::vector (one outlier of 4762.93x at large2) and 2.65x-3.63x faster than pmr::vector; emplace 1.20x-1.61x faster than std; selective construct path 1.21x-15.40x faster than std; churn simulation ranges from 1.58x slower to 1.66x faster than std; raw alloc 1.81x-287.40x faster than malloc.
compiler_and_flags: clang 20.1.8; -O3 -march=native -fstrict-aliasing -flto
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8840U, Arch Linux kernel 6.15.8, glibc 2.42 (ptmalloc), 64GB DDR5
tradeoffs: Compile-time fixed pool layout (metaset) must be tuned per workload; no general fallback beyond configured strides; header-only but requires C++23; cannot grow arbitrarily beyond the preallocated arena without a reset.
caveats: The ~1000x+ figures come only from the reserve microbenchmark, where each frame creates one std::vector, calls reserve(count), and frees it. glibc malloc/free of large blocks likely dominates that path, so it is not general alloc/free churn. In the more realistic tables the gains shrink to 1.2x-1.6x (emplace), and churn simulation is 1.06x-1.58x slower than std for 4096B and 16384B elements. Results are published only as a PNG image. New project (created Aug 2025, 37 stars) with no independent verification found.

name: Hoard
baseline: Solaris default allocator, Ptmalloc (glibc malloc backing operator new/delete)
workload: Uniprocessor and multiprocessor (1-14 way Sun Enterprise 5000) allocation-intensive benchmarks: threadtest, shbench, Larson server simulation, active/passive false-sharing tests, BEMengine PDE solver, Barnes-Hut n-body solver, plus single-threaded espresso/Ghostscript/LRUsim/p2c.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract: up to 60x over the standard Solaris allocator on 14 processors, and up to 18x over the next best allocator tested. At 14 processors: Larson 18x faster than Ptmalloc, threadtest 278% faster than Ptmalloc, shbench 85% faster than Ptmalloc. Uniprocessor: BEMengine 10.3% faster than the Solaris allocator, but the average over the uniprocessor benchmarks is 6.2% slower than Solaris.
compiler_and_flags: GNU C++ at -O6 (Sun Workshop C++ compiler 5.0 used only for Barnes-Hut)
hardware: Sun Enterprise 5000, 2GB RAM, 14x 400MHz UltraSPARC CPUs, 4MB L2 cache, Solaris 7
stars_or_usage: 1.25k stars; historically used by AOL, Cisco, SAP, Reuters, RBC and others per README; standard allocator option in SPEC CPU2006
tradeoffs: Multi-heap design trades some memory for scalability (bounded blowup, not zero); link-time/LD_PRELOAD drop-in malloc replacement, not a std::allocator template adapter; per-processor heap hashing can cause heap/thread collisions.
caveats: Primary evidence is the ASPLOS 2000 paper, run on 14x 400MHz UltraSPARC with Solaris 7 against the Solaris and Ptmalloc allocators of that era; the GNU C++ version is unstated. Uniprocessor, Hoard averaged 6.2% slower than the Solaris allocator (shbench +49.2%, espresso +15.9%, Ghostscript +10.6% runtime). The current README adds first-party modern results (code in benchmarks/, 192-core 2-node AMD EPYC, exact CPU model, compiler, and flags unstated, charts only). Those results claim 1.3-1.5x higher Larson throughput than glibc, mimalloc, and jemalloc, and 1.6x faster than glibc at 128 threads on NUMA. The README concedes that jemalloc wins linux-scalability. Hoard is also in daanx/mimalloc-bench as 'hd', but those results are chart images only.

workload: std::vector<TestClass>::emplace_back of 100 objects of sizes 8B-8KB, using a stack-backed bump-pointer Arena + ShortAlloc STL allocator vs the default heap allocator, measured on QuickBench (AWS-hosted).
claimed_speedup: Stack/arena allocator 2.2x-4.4x faster for objects up to 512B, and 93x-230x faster for 1KB-8KB objects (crossing glibc's mmap threshold)

name: atomic_queue
workload: SPSC round-trip ping-pong: 2 threads exchange a 4-byte int counter 1,000,000 times via two queue instances (lowest-contention case); also an N-producer/N-consumer throughput scalability test moving 1,000,000 messages through one queue, run across AMD Ryzen 5950X, Ryzen 5825U, Intel i9-9900KS and Intel Xeon Gold 6132.
claimed_speedup: Ping-pong latency on Ryzen 5950X (SMT): AtomicQueue mean 42ns vs std::mutex 320ns (~7.6x lower); OptimistAtomicQueue 33ns (~9.7x lower). 1-producer/1-consumer throughput on 5950X: AtomicQueue ~142.7M msg/s vs std::mutex ~4.1M msg/s (~34x); OptimistAtomicQueue mean ~1.23B msg/s (stdev ~136M, max ~2.04B). With 2-16 producer/consumer pairs, OptimistAtomicQueue stays ~4-24x ahead of std::mutex (52.9M vs 13.0M msg/s at 2; 55.3M vs 2.3M at 16), while plain AtomicQueue is roughly at parity with std::mutex.
compiler_and_flags: gcc-14.2.0 (Ryzen 5950X/5825U); gcc-8.4.0 (legacy i9-9900KS/Xeon Gold 6132). Current Makefile gcc release flags: -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -falign-functions=64 -DNDEBUG -fno-stack-protector -fno-stack-clash-protection -fno-tree-ch -fno-move-loop-invariants -fno-plt -fno-math-errno -ffinite-math-only -pthread; benchmarks.cc is compiled with -std=c++17, which is appended after the base -std=c++14.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5950X and Ryzen 5825U (KDE Neon/Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, mitigations=off); legacy: Intel i9-9900KS (Kubuntu 18.04) and Intel Xeon Gold 6132 (RHEL 6.10)
stars_or_usage: 1.9k stars; packaged in Conan Center and vcpkg
tradeoffs: Fixed capacity set at compile/construction time (ring buffer, no heap growth); no OS-blocking wait, only busy-spin (push/pop can't sleep, unsuitable for non-latency-critical code that wants to yield the CPU); atomic-element variants reserve a NIL sentinel value that must never be pushed; value-semantics only (copies/moves elements, no in-place references).
caveats: The 'std::mutex' baseline is atomic_queue's own fixed-size ring buffer guarded by std::mutex (AtomicQueueMutex), polled through try_push/try_pop retry loops. It is not std::queue with a condition variable. The ~1.23B msg/s 1P/1C OptimistAtomicQueue figure varies a lot (stdev ~136M, max ~2.04B). The page says throughput exceeds the inverse of latency on purpose, because the throughput loop has no dependency chains. Treat the 7.6-9.7x latency figures as the conservative claim. With 2+ producer/consumer pairs on the 5950X, plain AtomicQueue is roughly at parity with std::mutex: std::mutex leads at 2 pairs (13.0M vs 10.1M msg/s) and ties at 4. name: reckless
workload: Caller-side log-call latency in four scenarios. (1) Single-threaded periodic calls that never fill the buffer. (2) A call burst that fills the buffer. (3) Disk I/O: 2048 log entries interleaved with writing 64 GiB of data. (4) A Mandelbrot computation that logs ~1M lines with 1-8 worker threads (total runtime over 100 runs, overhead vs no-op). Baselines are std::fstream (std::flush after each line) and fprintf (fflush after each call), plus spdlog, g3log and Boost.Log.
claimed_speedup: Relative average call latency (reckless = 1.00). Periodic calls: fstream 41.32, stdio 43.77, spdlog 40.85, boost_log 67.42, g3log 78.19. Call burst: spdlog 1.93, fstream 2.36, stdio 2.55. Disk I/O: stdio 17.01, spdlog 23.82, fstream 5719.93. Mandelbrot overhead: single thread fstream 10.73, stdio 12.21, spdlog 9.21; 8 threads fstream 4.62, stdio 3.70. The page concludes: 'For low loads, the speed advantage over a simple fprintf can be a factor of 40.'
compiler_and_flags: gcc 7.3.0 (stated on the benchmark page). The benchmarks are built with tup (benchmarks/Tupfile.lua + Tuprules.lua), which on Linux compiles with g++ -O3 -ggdb3 -std=c++11 -Wall -Werror unless DEBUG=yes (then -O0). The page itself does not restate the flags.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 2700X @ 3.7GHz, 8 cores (SMT off); Samsung 970 EVO 1TB SSD (+ WD Red 3TB HDD for disk-I/O scenario); 32GB RAM; Linux kernel 4.14.65

name: SLEEF (SIMD Library for Evaluating Elementary Functions)
baseline: <cmath> (scalar libm, represented in the paper by FDLIBM as the reference scalar implementation)
workload: Reciprocal throughput (ns per call) of 256-bit vectorized double-precision SLEEF 3.4 (plus Vector-libm and Intel SVML) vs scalar FDLIBM 5.3. A single-threaded tight loop makes 10^10 calls over pre-generated, uniformly random arguments in each listed domain. The calling loop was compiled without optimization so calls are not elided (the libraries use their -O3 flags), and it is timed with clock_gettime.
claimed_speedup: Table 2, reciprocal throughput in ns per call, 1-ulp variants. SLEEF is the 256-bit AVX2 vectorized function (each call evaluates 4 doubles); FDLIBM 5.3 is scalar (1 value per call). sin [0,1e+100]: FDLIBM 162.3 vs SLEEF 48.79 (~3.3x per call). cos [0,1e+100]: 162.1 vs 50.38 (~3.2x). tan [0,1e+100]: 177.0 vs 48.82 (~3.6x). log [0,1e+300]: 31.66 vs 15.46 (~2.0x). exp [-700,700]: 12.19 vs 7.663 (~1.6x). pow: 69.40 vs 55.53 (~1.25x). On the fast-path domain [0.4,0.5], scalar FDLIBM is FASTER per call (sin 4.927 vs 11.43, cos 11.42 vs 13.75, tan 7.819 vs 17.30), as it is for acos (12.07 vs 16.09) and atan (10.16 vs 22.12). Per element (dividing by 4 lanes), SLEEF is faster in every 1-ulp row. (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: SLEEF and FDLIBM compiled with gcc-7.3.0 -O3 -mavx2 -mfma; Vector-libm compiled with gcc-7.3.0 -O3 -march=native -ftree-vectorize -ftree-vectorizer-verbose=1 -fno-math-errno; SVML via Intel C Compiler 19 with -fimf-max-error=1.0/4.0
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 CPU @ 3.40GHz, Turbo Boost disabled (physical PC, no VM)
tradeoffs: Vectorized code takes the slow path for a whole SIMD register if any lane needs it; library offers a 1-ULP and a faster 3.5-ULP accuracy tier as a speed/accuracy tradeoff; on narrow argument domains the scalar-equivalent speed roughly ties FDLIBM rather than beating it, the win is concentrated in wide-domain/branchy cases and true vector (multi-lane) throughput.
caveats: Table 2 compares SLEEF's 4-wide AVX2 vector functions against scalar FDLIBM. It is not a like-for-like scalar replacement of std::sin/std::exp: the gains need vectorized call sites, and SLEEF's scalar entry points are not in the table. Per call, FDLIBM beats vector SLEEF on narrow-domain sin/cos/tan and on acos/atan. FDLIBM is a reference libm, not glibc's libm or the libm behind libstdc++/libc++/MSVC <cmath>. The benchmark loop was built unoptimized for every library alike. The sleef.org benchmark page compares only against SVML. The Table 2 harness for FDLIBM is not in the repo.
